lesson_title: R5 to Play, R15 to Win — Do the Maths First
hook_text: Two coins. R5 to play, R15 if you get two heads. Sounds generous. Let's find out who's really winning.
clip_script: Two coins. Five rand to play, fifteen rand if both come up heads. Sounds generous. Let's check. First, what can actually happen? Coin one is heads or tails. For each of those, coin two is heads or tails. So: HH, HT, TH, TT. Four outcomes. And yes — heads-tails and tails-heads really are different, because they are different coins, even if it looks the same in your hand. That means two heads is one out of four. Twenty-five percent. Now the money. Imagine a hundred people play. The stall collects a hundred times five — five hundred rand. About twenty-five of them win, at fifteen rand each — that's three hundred and seventy-five paid out. The stall keeps a hundred and twenty-five rand out of every five hundred. Nothing is rigged. Nothing is hidden. The prize is just too small for the odds. So what would be fair? Five hundred rand shared among twenty-five expected winners is twenty rand. At R20, nobody wins in the long run. That one sum explains every raffle and every lottery you'll ever be offered.
visual_style: Two spinning coins landing into a four-square grid of outcomes, one square lighting gold; then two stacks of banknotes racing — R500 in, R375 out — with the R125 gap glowing at the stall's side of the table.
pacing: Playful setup, crisp four-outcome beat, decisive money reveal, calm final rule.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for tree diagrams, two-way tables and the whole 0-to-1 scale.
